introduction: These readings look forward: morals and intellects must change, spiritual perfections must catch up with material ones, a new race of men is forming, politicians will become spiritual and the wealthy unable to enjoy luxury beside want; and they ask their hearers to become that people now. Later passages add that the change is slow, passes through suffering, and reaches both inner life and outward conditions. Each of the sixty-five quotations is read here beside one from elsewhere. Most stand alongside: the prophets' new heart and new covenant, Paul's new creature, the leaven and the growing seed, Plato's philosopher-kings, Tennyson's Parliament of man, Hugo, the Universal Declaration. Nine push back or add a side: the Preacher sees nothing new under the sun, Kant and Jeremiah doubt that human beings can be remade, Nietzsche and Yeats imagine other new births, Wordsworth remembers a dawn that failed, and Mill speaks for the one who disagrees.
questions: The readings say that morals and even intellects must change. What change in yourself would count as evidence that this is possible?
Wordsworth thought the French Revolution a new dawn; Nietzsche announced a new man. What distinguishes the hope in these readings from earlier hopes that failed or did harm?
One reading foresees a time when a rich person cannot enjoy luxury while others lack bread. Dostoevsky's character loves humanity and not his neighbour. How does such sensitivity grow?
The later passages say that the change is gradual and comes through suffering. Does that make the vision more credible to you, or less?
Kant says that nothing straight can be made from such crooked material as man. What do the readings rely on that he leaves out?

outside.why: Bacon wrote that he that will not apply new remedies must expect new evils, for time is the greatest innovator.
Micah asks what the Lord requires but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God.
Jesus tells his hearers: ye are the light of the world; a city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
The Lord's Prayer asks that the kingdom come and the will be done in earth, as it is in heaven.
Daniel says that they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament.
Thoreau called our inventions pretty toys which distract our attention from serious things: improved means to an unimproved end.
Paul speaks of being changed into the same image from glory to glory.
James says: be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
Paul calls the law a schoolmaster to bring us onward, under whom we no longer are once faith is come.
The Song of Solomon sings that the winter is past, the rain is over and gone, and the flowers appear on the earth.
Isaiah says that the people that walked in darkness have seen a great light.
Ezekiel is told to call the breath from the four winds upon the slain, that they may live.
The Preacher says that there is no new thing under the sun: the thing that hath been, it is that which shall be. What would count as evidence that something new has entered human life?
Augustine prays: you have made us for yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in you.
Isaiah has God say: behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it?
The letter to the Hebrews begins: God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets.
Jesus likens the kingdom of heaven to leaven which a woman hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened.
John's Gospel says that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light.
John the Baptist says that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.
The psalm says: behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.
Paul writes that there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither bond nor free, neither male nor female, for all are one.
Jesus speaks of other sheep not of this fold, and of one fold and one shepherd.
Micah foresees every man sitting under his vine and under his fig tree, with none to make them afraid.
Paul speaks of putting on the new man, renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him.
Jesus says that men do not light a candle and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick.
Jesus says: I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled?
Jesus says that the earth bringeth forth fruit of herself: first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear.
Habakkuk says that the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.
Tennyson said of his own century of invention that knowledge comes, but wisdom lingers.
In the Revelation he that sat upon the throne says: behold, I make all things new.
Proverbs says: train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
Paul writes that if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away.
Plato held that until philosophers are kings, or kings have the spirit of philosophy, cities will never have rest from their evils.
Huxley held that the ethical progress of society depends not on imitating the cosmic process, but on combating it.
Jesus tells of a rich man who fared sumptuously every day while a beggar lay at his gate full of sores.
A character in Dostoevsky confesses: the more I love humanity in general, the less I love man in particular. What would have to change in a person before a neighbour's hunger spoiled his own dinner?
Tennyson foresaw the war-drum throbbing no longer in the Parliament of man, the Federation of the world.
Victor Hugo told a peace congress in 1849 that a day will come when the nations of the Continent are blended into a higher unity.
Yeats, looking at the same century, asked what rough beast, its hour come round at last, slouches towards Bethlehem to be born. Why do some see a new race forming and others a monster?

Wordsworth remembered the first days of the French Revolution: bliss was it in that dawn to be alive. He lived to see what followed. What protects the hope of a new dawn from the disappointments of earlier ones?
Nietzsche too announced a new kind of human being: man is a rope stretched between the animal and the Superman. What separates the new race these readings hope for from his?
Paul says that he counts not himself to have apprehended, but reaches forth unto those things which are before.
Jesus says: I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now.
Jesus says: seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you.
Paul asks his readers to present their bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God.
Jesus laments over Jerusalem, that killest the prophets and stonest them which are sent unto thee. What reason is there to think that a more enlightened world will receive its teachers better?
Peter's letter says that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.
Daniel tells of a stone cut out without hands that broke the great image in pieces and filled the whole earth.
Isaiah is sent to a people who hear indeed but understand not, and see indeed but perceive not.
Joel has God promise: I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy.
Jeremiah has God promise a new covenant: I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts.
Malachi says that the Lord shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver.
Kant remarked that out of such crooked material as man is made of, nothing can be hammered quite straight. How much can suffering, or anything else, remake human beings?
The letter to the Hebrews says that whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth.
Marx and Engels wrote of their own age that all that is solid melts into air, and all that is holy is profaned.
Shelley sings that the world's great age begins anew, and the golden years return.
Jesus says that a woman in travail hath sorrow, but afterwards remembereth no more the anguish, for joy that a child is born.
Samuel tells the king that to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.

Mill held that if all mankind minus one were of one opinion, mankind would be no more justified in silencing that one person than he in silencing mankind. What place has the one who disagrees in a community that is learning to obey its elected bodies?
The Universal Declaration of 1948 says that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights, and should act towards one another in a spirit of brotherhood.
Burke observed that a state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation.
James asks what it profits to say to the naked and hungry, be ye warmed and filled, and give them nothing.
Ezekiel has God promise: a new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.
Jeremiah asks whether the Ethiopian can change his skin or the leopard his spots. Is the transformation of inner life something a people can undertake, or only receive?
Paul exclaims at the depth of the wisdom of God: how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!
